claims.statement: The MCP server is one cheap-to-clone `OxyromonMcp` handler type holding the `SqlitePool`, a process `CancellationToken`, an `Arc<Mutex<()>>` write lock, a `read_only` flag and an optional `broadcast::Sender<SseMessage>`; the same handler backs both the stdio transport (`oxyromon mcp`) and the Streamable HTTP service `mcp_http_service` that `src/server.rs` nests at `/mcp`.

`mcp::main` serves `rmcp::transport::stdio()` and then waits in `tokio::select!` on `server.waiting()` (transport/EOF end) against Ctrl+C; Ctrl+C cancels the token to unwind in-flight mutating actions, and `src/main.rs` runs the server outside the single-connection subcommand scope before `optimize_database`.

Under `oxyromon mcp` or `/mcp`, stdout carries MCP JSON-RPC: never `println!`/`print!` from any code path the MCP server can reach — log (`log::*`) or use the `progress.rs` helpers, which write to stderr.

MCP write tools reuse the CLI subcommands rather than reimplementing them: seven build an argv vector and feed it to the subcommand's own clap `Command` via `try_get_matches_from` before calling its `main()` on a pooled connection — the same synthesized-`ArgMatches` trick `src/mutation.rs` GraphQL mutations use — so CLI, GraphQL and MCP cannot drift apart per surface; `download_dats`, `purge_systems` and `set_setting` call the underlying library entry points directly instead.

Every mutating tool funnels through `OxyromonMcp::run_action`, which takes the shared `write_lock` before acquiring one pooled connection and holds it across the whole action so SQLite writers queue explicitly instead of surfacing `SQLITE_BUSY`; because `OxyromonMcp::new` allocates a fresh lock and the HTTP factory builds a handler per request, the lock is globally effective under stdio but not between concurrent `/mcp` requests.

`run_action` creates a none-style `ProgressBar` (no TTY in MCP mode) that the subcommand owns and ticks; when — and only when — the caller supplied a `progressToken`, a spawned task polls the bar every 400 ms and emits `notifications/progress` only when `(position, length, message)` changes, aborting when the action settles or the notify fails.

A running MCP action races three futures in `tokio::select!`: the work closure, the per-request `ctx.ct` (yielding "cancelled by the client") and the server-level `cancel` token (yielding "server shutting down"), so both a disconnecting client and a stopping process unblock a long-running mutation.

When mounted on the web server and given an `sse_prefix`, `run_action` broadcasts `{prefix}_started` / `{prefix}_complete` / `{prefix}_error` on the SSE channel so a UI watching `/events` reacts to MCP-triggered work; `import_roms` and `set_setting` pass `sse_prefix: None` and emit nothing there.

`--read-only` is enforced by the router: `tool_router()` calls `disable_route` on every `write_router` tool before merging, so write tools disappear from `tools/list` and `tools/call` is rejected at the protocol level; the per-tool `read_only_denial` tool-error checks are secondary, and the HTTP factory always constructs with `read_only: false`, so `/mcp` exposes the write tools.

Destructive tools require an explicit `confirm: true`: `purge_systems` and `purge_irds` gate unconditionally while `purge_roms` gates only when `trash` or `foreign` is set (the file-deleting modes) and separately rejects a call with none of its four flags; refusal is the tool-level `need_confirm` result, and the synthesized argv appends `--yes` so the subcommands never block on a nonexistent TTY.

Tool results use three deliberate channels: `ok_json`/`ok_text` for success (structured `structuredContent` vs prose), `tool_error` (`isError: true`) for actionable refusals such as unknown ids, empty path lists, unknown formats and invalid setting values, and `Err(McpError)` only for things the server cannot route or serve (pool-acquire failure, unknown resource URI or its payload failing to serialize, `audit_system` on a missing system); a *tool* payload that fails to serialize degrades to `tool_error` inside `ok_json` rather than becoming a protocol error.

The read tools are all annotated `read_only_hint = true` and use their own pooled connections without the write lock, while write tools carry `idempotent_hint`, `open_world_hint` (`download_dats`) or `destructive_hint` (the three purges); JSON Schema for every tool derives from the `params.rs` structs whose doc comments are the prose the model reads.

Tool/resource payloads use compact `output.rs` structs — snake_case, enum names instead of stored integers, no unusable bookkeeping ids — because every field lands in a model's context window; read paging is clamped server-side (list_games default 100 / cap 1000, search_games default 50 / cap 500), and `status` plus the `oxyromon://status` resource share `build_status` which reports dependency availability with a null version when a codec is missing.

A tool's `system_id` is resolved by `require_system` into the system's name because that is what the CLI subcommands accept (`--system`), and an unknown id returns the tool-level error 'system N not found; list_systems has the ids' pointing at the tool that has the ids.

The server exposes `oxyromon://status`, `oxyromon://systems`, `oxyromon://settings` plus one dynamically listed `oxyromon://systems/{id}` per system (with `{system_id}` registered as a resource template), returning JSON text and a protocol `resource_not_found` for unknown URIs; after mutations it sends `notify_resource_updated` for a single touched system or `notify_resources_changed` when the system set may have changed.

The two prompts `onboard_system` and `audit_system` are not generic templates: each queries the database first and embeds a real library snapshot, with `onboard_system` branching on whether the system already exists and, if not, whether it is a Redump system to choose `download_dats` versus `import_dats` as step 1.

The Cargo feature `mcp = ["dep:rmcp", "dep:schemars"]` builds only the stdio server and `server` implies `mcp` plus `rmcp/transport-streamable-http-server`; building with `mcp` also changes `establish_connection` via `cfg_if` to five connections with `PRAGMA locking_mode = NORMAL` instead of the CLI's single `EXCLUSIVE` connection, and CI compiles the stdio-only combination with `cargo clippy --no-default-features --features use-rustls,mcp --all-targets`.

`tests/mcp_stdio.rs` (`#![cfg(feature = "mcp")]`) spawns the real `oxyromon mcp` binary and drives it with raw line-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout — no SDK client — asserting the wire format plus the full tool/prompt/resource lists, `structuredContent` reads, unknown-id tool errors, purge confirm gating, CLI-mirroring setting validation, and that `--read-only` both hides and refuses write tools; it also proves the server exits successfully on stdin EOF.

Write-tool argument validation runs in the handler *before* `run_action`, on its own short-lived pooled connection: `sort_roms`/`check_roms` require exactly one of `system_id` or `all: true`, `purge_roms` rejects a call with none of `missing`/`orphan`/`trash`/`foreign`, `import_dats`/`import_roms`/`download_dats` reject empty path or system lists, and `convert_roms` checks the format against `convert_roms::ALL_FORMATS` plus the arcade restriction. A malformed call therefore returns immediately instead of queueing behind the write lock held by a long-running action.

The synthesized argv encodes MCP's headless defaults, which diverge from the interactive CLI: `import_roms` always appends `--unattended` (defaulting to `first`, so the CLI's prompting `none` mode is unreachable from MCP), `purge_irds` always passes `--system` — which is what makes `purge-irds` purge every IRD game unattended instead of prompting per game — and `sort_roms`/`purge_roms` append `--yes`, the only two subcommands the MCP surface reaches that declare a `YES` prompt-skipping flag.
